lines.L1: It's the worst night of the storm. Rosa's mother is on oxygen. The battery says ten percent. Rosa calls nine-one-one... and waits.
lines.L2: In Hurricane Harvey, Houston's nine-one-one took seventy-five thousand calls in three days. A normal day? Eight thousand. The line is the bottleneck.
lines.L3: But help was already there. After Superstorm Sandy, two in three people said their neighbors helped them recover. Help is blocks away. Nothing connects it.
lines.L4: So Rosa opens ReliefSync, and just talks. In seconds, an A.I. agent understands the emergency, rates it life-threatening, finds her street, and sees the flood cutting off the main road.
lines.L5: Now, the marketplace. The dispatcher broadcasts a request. Every nearby volunteer has an agent that answers, with a price, an arrival time, and a track record.
lines.L6: Maya's four-by-four is four minutes away. Lena, a nurse, volunteers for free, but she's twenty-two minutes out. Diego's boat is too slow. Sam's battery is low.
lines.L7: Seven factors, scored live. For a life-threatening call, there's no haggling. Maya wins, in about a second.
lines.L8: For routine needs, the agents negotiate. Price, quality, track record, inside a relief-fund cap. Offer. Counter. Deal.
lines.L9: Six seconds after the S.O.S., Maya's phone buzzes. One tap. The route runs around the flood, on real streets.
lines.L10: Nine minutes later, the power is back on. And Rosa's data is erased.
lines.L11: Not a bulletin board. An autonomous dispatcher, that turns neighbors into first responders.
lines.L12: ReliefSync. Every call for help, answered in seconds.
